Sequence [2,3]-Sigmatropic Rearrangement: One-Pot Synthesis of 
Propargyl Allenylamines 
Huihui Feng,‡,a Yujuan Xie,‡,a Liliang Huang,a Yongqing Xu,a Junhai Huang,*,a and Huangdi Feng*,a,b 
a College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Shanghai University of Engineering Science, Shanghai 201620, China 
b Shanghai Frontiers Science Research Center for Druggability of Cardiovascular noncoding RNA, Institute for Frontier Medical Technology, 
 Shanghai University of Engineering Science, Shanghai 201620, China 
Keywords 
Allene | Propargylamine | C—N activation | Sigmatropic rearrangement | Metal-free | Synthetic methods | Domino reactions 
Comprehensive Summary  
 
Allenes, served as highly sought -after building blocks, are an indispensable component of synthetic chemistry. Their utility in mod u-
lating the chemical, physical, and pharmaceutical properties of organic compounds make allenes a desirable choice in various applic a-
tions. Here , we report a facile method for the atom -economical synthesis of propargyl allenylamines via an underdeveloped 
[2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement. Our strategy employs easily accessible propargylamines as starting materials, which are first co n-
verted into propargyl ammonium salts, followed by a base -promoted [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement. This one -pot, two-step reac-
tion proceeds in the ab sence of transition metals, displays a very broad scope, and does not require the introduction of the ele c-
tron-withdrawing group into the starting materials.

 Concise Report Feng et al. 
Background and Originality Content 
Allenes and their derivatives, which are powerful and versatile 
building blocks in synthetic chemistry, have been widely used for 
the synthesis of various biologically active heterocycles and 
structurally-complex molecules. [1] These compounds also have a 
broad spectrum of biological activities and are found in a large 
number of natural products  such as enprostil, mycomycin, 
acalycixeniolides E, archangiumide,  and so on. [2] Consequently, a 
number of synthetic approaches have been established to con -
struct allene -containing m olecules.[3] Notably, transition metal - 
mediated allenation of terminal alkynes via subsequent 1,5 -H 
transfer-β-elimination[4] and transition metal -catalyzed electro -
philic substitutions of different propargylic  electrophiles[5] repre-
sent the elegant stra tegies towards a diverse range of allene 
compounds. 
In recent years, molecular rearrangements such as [2,3] -sig-
matropic rearrangement and Claisen rearrangement have been 
successively developed to prepare functionalized allenes with high 
atom- and step -economy.[6] In this field, the [2,3] -sigmatropic 
rearrangement of propargylamines is an enduring challenge and 
has attracted considerable attention. In such processes, a specific 
type of allene, called allenylamine, is produced by the use of dif -
ferent reacti on systems. For example, in 2018, Tian and 
co-workers reported a benzyne -mediated [2,3] -sigmatropic rear -
rangement of tertiary propargylamines to synthesize allenyla -
mines using 2 -(trimethylsilyl)aryl triflate as an aryne precursor 
(Scheme 1a).[7] In the same year, Song and co-workers disclosed a 
catalytic asymmetric [2,3] -sigmatropic rearrangement of propar -
gyl ammonium salts in the presence of the chiral isothiourea cat -
alyst (Scheme 1b).[8] More recently, a sequence of MgI2-promoted 
ring opening of cyclopropyl ketones and base-promoted [2,3]-sig-
matropic rearrangement of propargyl ammonium ylides has been 
developed by the Zhang group, yielding a variety of allenyl -sub-
stituted indolizidines (Scheme 1c). [9a] However, these methods 
rely on the introduc tion of electron -withdrawing groups at the 
α-position of the nitrogen atom and typically exploit the acidity of 
the C−H group next to an electron -withdrawing group functionali-
ty for domino deprotonation/[2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement. It 
is noteworthy th at the [2,3] -sigmatropic rearrangement, which 
only involves less acidic propargylamine derivatives and avoids the 
substitution pattern of the electron -withdrawing group, remains 
an uncharted territory. 
Inspired by our recent study on the chemical transform ations  
Scheme 1  [2,3]-Sigmatropic rearrangement of propargylaime derivative 
 
of propargylamines, [10] we envisaged that the synthesis of s truc-
turally diverse allenylamines could be achieved by molecular re-
arrangement of functionalized propargylamines. In this article, we 
disclose a sequential strategy of nucleophilic substitution of di -
propargylamines with methyl trifluoromethanesulfonate (MeOTf) 
and [2,3] -sigmatropic rearrangement of quaternary propargylic  
ammonium ylides under mild conditions (Scheme 1d). This pro -
tocol correctly employs the appropriate dipropargylamines as 
starting materials, which can aid in the development of an effi -
cient [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement without the introduction of 
the electron-withdrawing groups. The study represents the first 
example of the molecular rearrangement of dipropargylamine, 
leading to the generation of propargyl allenylamines in a one -pot 
manner . The synergistic effect of the allene and propargyl func-
tional groups may allow this type of compound to be considered 
as a unique functionality with special reactivity.[11] 
Results and Discussion 
To evaluate the feasibility of the reaction, we initially synthe -
sized the model substrate, dipropargyl ammonium salt  2a, 
through a copper -catalyzed A3-coupling reaction to obtain dipro -
pargylamine,[12] which was then followed by a nucleophilic sub -
stitution with MeOTf. [13] Subsequently, compound 2a was intro -
duced into the reaction system under the catalyst-free conditions, 
leading to the formation of the desired product 3a in 17% yield in 
the presence of KOH (1.0 equiv) and tetrahydrofuran (THF) at 
65 °C for 6 h (Table 1, entry 1).  Buoyed by this initial succ ess, a 
series of solvents were tested to optimize the yield of product 3a 
(entries 2 —4). The results revealed that toluene was  the most 
effective solvent, delivering a 22% yield of the target product (en -
try 4).  Next, various bas es including NaOH, Na2CO3, and t-BuOK 
were screened (entries 5—7). t-BuOK was identified to be optimal, 
providing 3a in 54% yield (entry 7). To our delight, the yield of the 
product 3a was further improved to 75% when the amount of 
t-BuOK was reduced to 0.8 equiv (entries 8 and 9). However, fur-
ther optimization of reaction parameters was not effective in 
promoting the reaction (entries 10—13). For example, modulating 
the reaction temperature resulted in the generation of desired

 One-Pot Synthesis of Propargyl Allenylamines Chin. J. Chem.

a Reaction conditions: propargylamines 1 (0.5 mmol), MeOTf (1.0 mmol) stirred in Et2O (4 mL) for 20 min at 0 °C, then removing Et2O and adding t-BuOK 
(0.8 mmol), toluene (2 mL), the mixture stirred for 6 h at 65 °C; Isolated yield.
product 3a in 65% and 55% yields, respectively (entries 10 and 11). 
Changing the reaction time led to a significant decrease in the 
yield to 23% and 40%, respectively  (entries 12 and 13). Further -
more, a reduction in the yield of 3a was observed when the reac-
tion was conducted in a nitrogen atmosphere (entry 14). 
Having established the optimal reaction parameters, we ex -
plored its versatility in the [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement using 
a diverse array of propargylamines 1 via a one -pot, two-step pro-
cedure. As depicted in Scheme 2, our approach exhibited a robust 
tolerance for various functional groups and generated the desired 
products 3a—3q in moderate to good yields. For example, pro -
pargylamines bearing different R 2 groups, including straight-chain 
alkyl (propyl, butyl, amyl), branched alkyl (iospropyl), and cycloal -
kyl (cyclopentyl), proceeded smoothly to deliver the correspond -
ing products 3a—3e in good yields. Furthermore, a variety of 
R1-substituted propargylamin es were screened and the reaction 
worked efficiently to give the desired products 3f—3l in moderate 
to good yields. In these cases, both electron -withdrawing and 
electron-donating functional groups, including the synthetically 
useful bromo substituent, wer e accommodated in the different 
positions of the benzene ring, while the nitro -subsitituted sub -
strate led to the formation of 3l in a slightly reduced yield. To fur-
ther investigate the functional group tolerance of the method, 
other R 1- and R 2-substituted propargylamines were introduced 
into the reaction. The results showed that these substrates were 
compatible with the reaction, allowing the synthesis of the target 
products 3m—3q in good yields. 
In addition, when the ethyl trifluoromethanesulfonate ( EtOTf) 
was chosen as the alkylation reagent, the desired [2,3]-sigma-
tropic rearrangement  product 4 was obtained in 60% yield 
(Scheme 3a). Unsymmetrical dipropargyl ammonium salt was also 
applicable, however, leading to the formation of a mixture of two 
regioisomers 5 and 5’ in 42% yield (Scheme 3b).

Based on our experimental observations and the previous lit -
erature,[7,9] we proposed a plausible reaction pathway (Scheme 4). 
At f irst, the reaction began with the generation of di propargyl 
ammonium salt 2 through a nucleophilic substitution of dipropar-
gylamine 1 with methyl trifluoromethanesulfonate . Then, the 
intermediate 2 underwent deprotonation to form quaternary 
dipropargylic ammonium ylide A in the presence of t-BuOK. Finally, 
the [2,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement of ylide A was achieved 
through a converted five-membered transition state B, resulting in 
the formation of the desired product 3. 
Scheme 4  Plausible reaction pathway 
 
Conclusions 
In summary, we have established a unique [2,3]-sigmatropic 
rearrangement of di propargylamines, which is currently under -
developed, offering a straightforward  and modular method for 
the synthesis of a wi de range of propargyl allenylamines. Our 
research reveals an atom-economical and versatile reaction with a 
broad scope of substrates without the introduction of the elec -
tron-withdrawing groups, outstanding efficiency, and high chemo-
selectivity. The disti nctive combination of propargyl and allenyl 
groups holds substantial potential as a robust framework for the 
construction of valuable compounds.
